title: Logging in with cookies
idea: Login trades a correct email and password for two tokens. The server sets them as `httpOnly` cookies and saves the refresh token on the user.
points: Find the user by email, then compare the password with the stored hash.
Unknown email and wrong password both get `401` with one message.
The refresh token is saved on the user; the access token is not.
`httpOnly` hides a cookie from page scripts; `secure` limits it to HTTPS.

walk.text: Find the user by email. A missing user and a wrong password throw the same `401`.
Make both tokens. Only the refresh token is saved on the user.
Read the user back without the secret fields.
One options object, shared by both cookies. `secure` turns on in production.
Set both cookies with the same options. The body carries the user, no tokens.
A real login: body keys, `Set-Cookie` headers with token values hidden, and the saved refresh token.
A wrong password, an unknown email, then production mode, which adds `Secure`.

pitfalls: Pass the same options to both `.cookie()` calls; options apply to one cookie only.
Do not repeat the tokens in the JSON body: page scripts could read them.
Validate the body (next lesson): an object-valued `email` can act as a query operator.

quiz.why: Options belong to one `.cookie()` call. Only `a` got `httpOnly`, so `b` has no `HttpOnly` flag. Each cookie is its own header.

takeaway: Check the password once; afterwards the cookies speak for the user.

starters: Why save the refresh token in the database?
Why is the access token not stored?
Can a non-browser client use these cookies?
